summary: The eternal security of the believer; assurance grounded in God’s promises, the Spirit’s witness, and the fruits of faith
readingInstruction: Read John 10:27-30, Romans 8:31-39, and 1 John 5:11-13. Today is a doctrinal pause on perseverance and assurance. Notice the language of security and the repeated phrase “no one” and “nothing” can separate us from Christ.
settingTheScene: Two questions trouble many Christians. First: can a true believer lose his salvation? Second: how can I know that I am really saved? The first is the doctrine of perseverance, and the second is the doctrine of assurance. They are related but distinct. Christians have answered them in different ways, so we proceed carefully and with charity, and we let Scripture speak.
observation: “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me” (John 10:27).
“I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28).
“No one is able to snatch them out of the Father’s hand” (John 10:29).
“If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31).
“Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?” (Romans 8:35).
“Will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:39).
“Whoever has the Son has life” (1 John 5:12).
“I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God that you may know that you have eternal life” (1 John 5:13).
doctrinalFocus:
Perseverance of the saints is the teaching that all those truly born again will be kept by God and will persevere in faith to the end. They are kept not by their own strength but by God’s power (1 Peter 1:5). Those who fall away finally show they were never truly of us (1 John 2:19). This is the view of Reformed churches and of many Baptists and other evangelicals, sometimes expressed as “eternal security” or “once saved, always saved,” though the first phrase is better because it stresses that true believers do persevere.

The case for perseverance rests on the promises of God. Jesus says his sheep “will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.” Paul says that those God predestined, he called; those he called, he justified; and those he justified, he glorified (Romans 8:30), with no loss along the chain. He is “sure that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers… will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.” Philippians 1:6 promises that he who began a good work will bring it to completion. Jude 24 says he is able to keep us from stumbling. Salvation depends on God’s faithfulness, not ours.

Other Christians, especially in Arminian and Wesleyan traditions, hold that a true believer can, through persistent unbelief and rejection of Christ, fall from grace. They point to warning passages such as Hebrews 6:4-6, 10:26-31, and 2 Peter 2:20-22, and to Jesus’ words in John 15:1-6 about branches that do not abide. Many in this tradition affirm that believers have a strong security in Christ and that falling away is not a casual matter, but rather a deliberate abandonment of faith. Both sides take the warnings seriously. The Reformed answer is that the warnings are real means God uses to keep his people persevering: they are warnings to those who profess faith but may not have it, and they are God’s way of causing true believers to hold fast. Perseverance is something believers do, empowered by God.

Assurance is the confidence that I am a child of God. John says this is the purpose of his letter (1 John 5:13). Assurance rests on three supports. First, the promises of God in Scripture: whoever believes in him has eternal life. Second, the inward witness of the Holy Spirit, who testifies with our spirit that we are children of God (Romans 8:16). Third, the fruit in our lives: growing love, obedience, and hatred of sin. A person may be truly saved but lack assurance for a time, because of sin, depression, or weak understanding. Assurance can grow, and it is a gift to pray for.

How should we hold the doctrine? With humility and care. The warnings keep us from presumption, and the promises keep us from despair. A believer who struggles with doubt should look away from his own performance to Christ, who holds him. A person who is careless should hear the warnings. Our confidence is not in our grip on Christ, but in his grip on us.
interpretation:
In John 10, Jesus describes his sheep: they hear his voice, he knows them, and they follow him. Note that the description includes following, which is a mark of true sheep. He gives them eternal life, and they will never perish. The security is double: they are in his hand and in the Father’s hand. The ground is that “I and the Father are one”: the power that holds us is the unlimited power of God.

Romans 8 builds an argument from God’s love. If God gave his own Son for us, will he not give us all things? Who will bring a charge against God’s elect? God is the one who justifies. Who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died, who was raised, who is at the right hand of God, who intercedes for us. Then the great list of possible threats: tribulation, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, danger, sword; death, life, angels, rulers, things present, things to come, powers, height, depth, anything else in all creation. None can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord. This is a promise for those in Christ and rests on what Christ has done.

First John 5 ties assurance to the possession of the Son. “And this is the testimony, that God gave us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life.” The question is whether we have the Son. If we believe in his name, we have life, and God wants us to know it.
connection: Philippians 1:6 and Jude 24-25 promise God’s keeping. 1 Peter 1:3-5 says we are guarded by God’s power through faith. Ephesians 1:13-14 says we are sealed with the Spirit. Romans 8:28-30 gives the golden chain. John 6:37-40 and 17:11-12 speak of Jesus keeping those the Father gave him. Hebrews 3:12-14, 6:4-12, and 10:26-39 are warnings. John 15:1-8 speaks of abiding. Colossians 1:21-23 calls for continuing in the faith. 2 Peter 1:10 urges making our calling and election sure. Romans 8:16 speaks of the Spirit’s witness. 2 Corinthians 13:5 urges self-examination.
application:
If you doubt your salvation, take your eyes off yourself and look at Christ. Read John 10:27-30 slowly and rest.

If you have grown careless, hear the warnings kindly and ask whether you are abiding in Christ daily.

Share 1 John 5:13 with a struggling friend and pray that they would know they have eternal life.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus, the Good Shepherd, for keeping you.
Thank him that nothing can separate you from his love.
Ask him to strengthen your assurance.
